subject: Great White Shark
fact: Great white sharks can detect tiny electrical signals made by other animals.

subject: Whale Shark
fact: Whale sharks are the largest fish in the world and eat mostly tiny plankton.

subject: Hammerhead Shark
fact: Hammerhead sharks have wide heads that help them sense and locate prey.

subject: Tiger Shark
fact: Tiger sharks have dark vertical stripes when they are young.

subject: Bull Shark
fact: Bull sharks can swim in both salt water and fresh water.

subject: Nurse Shark
fact: Nurse sharks often rest on the seafloor during the day.

subject: Blacktip Reef Shark
fact: Blacktip reef sharks are named for the dark tips on several of their fins.

subject: Whitetip Reef Shark
fact: Whitetip reef sharks often rest in caves or under ledges.

subject: Lemon Shark
fact: Lemon sharks have yellow-brown coloring that helps them blend with sandy water.

subject: Shortfin Mako Shark
fact: Shortfin mako sharks are among the fastest sharks in the ocean.

subject: Thresher Shark
fact: Thresher sharks have extremely long upper tail fins.

subject: Goblin Shark
fact: Goblin sharks have long snouts and jaws that can extend forward quickly.

subject: Basking Shark
fact: Basking sharks are giant filter feeders that strain plankton from seawater.

subject: Greenland Shark
fact: Greenland sharks are among the longest-lived vertebrate animals.

subject: Blue Shark
fact: Blue sharks have slim bodies and long pointed pectoral fins.

subject: Zebra Shark
fact: Young zebra sharks have stripes while adults develop spots.

subject: Epaulette Shark
fact: Epaulette sharks can use their fins to walk across shallow reef flats.

subject: Wobbegong
fact: Wobbegongs are flat bottom-dwelling sharks with camouflage patterns.

subject: Cookiecutter Shark
fact: Cookiecutter sharks remove small round bites from larger animals.

subject: Port Jackson Shark
fact: Port Jackson sharks have blunt heads and strong teeth for crushing shellfish.

subject: Horn Shark
fact: Horn sharks have short blunt heads and spines in front of their dorsal fins.

subject: Angel Shark
fact: Angel sharks have flattened bodies that make them look a little like rays.

subject: Sawshark
fact: Sawsharks have long toothed snouts used to help find and stun prey.

subject: Dogfish Shark
fact: Dogfish sharks are small sharks that often travel in groups.

subject: Bonnethead Shark
fact: Bonnetheads are small relatives of hammerhead sharks with shovel-shaped heads.

subject: Silky Shark
fact: Silky sharks are named for the smooth texture of their skin.

subject: Oceanic Whitetip Shark
fact: Oceanic whitetip sharks have broad rounded fins with pale tips.

subject: Spinner Shark
fact: Spinner sharks can leap from the water while spinning.

subject: Sand Tiger Shark
fact: Sand tiger sharks can look fierce but usually swim slowly and calmly.

subject: Frilled Shark
fact: Frilled sharks have eel-like bodies and rows of needle-shaped teeth.

subject: Giant Manta Ray
fact: Giant manta rays can have wingspans wider than a small car.

subject: Reef Manta Ray
fact: Reef manta rays often visit cleaning stations where small fish remove parasites.

subject: Spotted Eagle Ray
fact: Spotted eagle rays have long tails and white spots across their backs.

subject: Southern Stingray
fact: Southern stingrays often bury themselves in sand with only their eyes showing.

subject: Round Stingray
fact: Round stingrays have nearly circular bodies and short tails.

subject: Blue-Spotted Ribbontail Ray
fact: Blue-spotted ribbontail rays have bright spots and usually rest near reefs.

subject: Cownose Ray
fact: Cownose rays often swim together in large groups.

subject: Bat Ray
fact: Bat rays use strong jaws to crush clams crabs and other hard-shelled food.

subject: Electric Ray
fact: Electric rays can produce electrical shocks to defend themselves or stun prey.

subject: Butterfly Ray
fact: Butterfly rays have wide wing-like fins and very short tails.

subject: Guitarfish
fact: Guitarfish have flattened fronts like rays and shark-like tails.

subject: Shovelnose Ray
fact: Shovelnose rays have pointed snouts and long narrow bodies.

subject: Sawfish
fact: Sawfish are rays with long toothed snouts called rostra.

subject: Skate
fact: Skates lay egg cases sometimes called mermaid's purses.

subject: Thornback Skate
fact: Thornback skates have rough spines along their backs and tails.

subject: Little Skate
fact: Little skates are small bottom-dwelling relatives of rays.

subject: Devil Ray
fact: Devil rays are close relatives of manta rays and swim with wing-like fins.

subject: Mobula Ray
fact: Mobula rays sometimes leap completely out of the water.

subject: Pelagic Stingray
fact: Pelagic stingrays live in open ocean rather than staying on the seafloor.

subject: Yellow Stingray
fact: Yellow stingrays have round bodies with spotted or mottled patterns.

subject: Atlantic Stingray
fact: Atlantic stingrays can enter brackish and freshwater areas.

subject: Freshwater Stingray
fact: Freshwater stingrays live in rivers and lakes in South America.

subject: Porcupine Ray
fact: Porcupine rays have rough skin covered with small thorn-like bumps.

subject: Sixgill Stingray
fact: Sixgill stingrays are unusual rays with six pairs of gill slits.

subject: Shark Ray
fact: Shark rays have broad ray-like heads and powerful shark-like tails.

subject: Bowmouth Guitarfish
fact: Bowmouth guitarfish have broad heads covered with rows of small ridges.

subject: Common Skate
fact: Common skates are large skates that live on the seafloor.

subject: Manta Ray Pup
fact: Manta ray babies are born live and are called pups.

subject: Baby Shark
fact: Young sharks are called pups and many are born ready to swim on their own.

subject: Ray Pup
fact: Many young rays are born as small live pups shaped like tiny adults.
